dept.tagline: Two degrees, one department: the 120-credit BSS in Economics and the 130-credit BSS in Anthropology, each on its own map with every printed prerequisite, the thesis route as each programme prints it, and a tracker that does the CGPA math on BRACU's own scale.

skills: Year 1
Economics: supply and demand, costs and the national accounts drawn and shifted without notes (ECO 101, ECO 102), and the mathematics that carries them (MAT 101, then ECO 201).
Anthropology: the vocabulary of the discipline and a first ethnography read as an argument, not a story (ANT 101, ANT 104 Biological Anthropology, ANT 201 Language, Society and Culture).
Reading with a pencil: every chapter reduced to its argument in five lines, from the first semester.
Writing that gets to the point: the two Writing courses (ENG 101 / ENG 102 / ENG 103, by placement) used on the essays your major sets.
Year 2

Economics: the intermediate sequence worked through problem sets (ECO 206, ECO 207, then ECO 208 and ECO 209 - the pair almost every elective asks for) and statistics you can run (ECO 202, then ECO 303 Introduction to Econometrics).
Anthropology: the theory spine begun - ANT 202 / SOC 201 Inequality and Power, ANT 203 / SOC 301 Social Theory, ANT 301 History of Anthropological Thought - with a reading response for every seminar.
A spreadsheet and one statistics package, used on real Bangladesh data.
A two-page essay or policy memo with one table or chart, written to a word limit.
Year 3

Economics: the applied core (ECO 308 International Trade, ECO 309 Public Finance, ECO 311 Economic Growth and Development, ECO 324 Bangladesh Economy, ECO 431, ECO 432) and the first elective choices pointed one way.

Anthropology: ANT 302 Contemporary Issues in Anthropological Theory, then the applied core (ANT 320, ANT 321 Economy and Society, ANT 330 Anthropology of Development, ANT 350 Gender and Society) and the first of five electives.
A field observation or a small dataset written up with evidence, and a literature review that argues rather than lists.
Department seminars attended with a note of the method each speaker used; the department runs an ESS Working Paper Series.
Year 4
Economics: ECO 401 Research Methods (seminar papers), ECO 430 Econometric Analysis or ECO 307 Mathematical Methods, and the two-semester ECO 499 Undergraduate Thesis if a supervisor takes you on.

Anthropology: ANT 375 Reading Ethnography and ANT 376 Research Methodology back to back, then the three-month ANT 401 (b) thesis or ANT 402 (b) internship with its proposal, progress and final defences.
Presenting results to non-specialists in five minutes, and defending them for thirty.
Applications for jobs, competitive examinations or graduate programmes, with the thesis or internship report as your writing sample.
dept.career_intro: Two degrees share this department. The BSS in Economics (120 credits) is 16 core courses of theory, mathematics and econometrics plus eleven electives; the BSS in Anthropology (130 credits) is a theory spine, a research-methods pair and a thesis or internship, with seven open electives that 'can be a minor'. The Economics page lists development organisations, higher education, teaching and research, finance and banking, public policy, market research, financial analysis, management consulting, data analysis, entrepreneurship and the civil service; the Anthropology page lists anthropological research, social services, museums and heritage, digital anthropology and UX research, business and marketing, and teaching. None of it is a BRACU rule.
careers: Development organisations and NGOs
Programme, research, monitoring and evaluation roles with NGOs, donors and international agencies - the direction both programme pages name first.

Economics: ECO 311, ECO 322 Gender and Development, ECO 421 Welfare Economics and Development, ECO 422 Human Capital and Development. Anthropology: ANT 330 Anthropology of Development, ANT 350, the ANT 402 (b) internship (the page names research organisations, NGOs and donors).
Banks, finance and financial analysis
Credit, treasury, research and trainee tracks in banks and non-bank financial institutions.
ECO 432 Money and Banking, ECO 431 International Finance and Economic Policy, ECO 331 Corporate Economics and Finance, spreadsheets, recruitment-test preparation.
Public policy, central banking and regulators
Economic analysis and policy work in ministries, the central bank and regulators.
ECO 309 Public Finance, ECO 324 Bangladesh Economy, ECO 312 Cost Benefit Analysis, ECO 325 Political Economic Analysis, econometrics you can defend.
Research, think tanks and higher study
Policy and academic research; a master's or PhD (the department runs an MS in Applied Economics).
CGPA, ECO 401, ECO 430, ECO 499 or ECO 498; for Anthropology ANT 375, ANT 376, ANT 418 Senior Seminar and the ANT 401 (b) thesis; a writing sample and two faculty referees.
Data analysis and market research
Analyst roles that prize statistics, survey design and clear writing.
ECO 202, ECO 303, ECO 430 and a statistics package; ANT 376 Research Methodology's questionnaires, sampling and analysis software; one dataset project you can show.
Digital anthropology and UX research
User, product and design research in technology and media firms - a direction the Anthropology page names.
ANT 211 Anthropology of Social Media, ANT 204 Social Transformation in the Digital Age, ANT 210 Anthropology of Corporate Culture, interview practice from ANT 376.
Social services, museums and heritage
Case work, community programmes, heritage and cultural institutions.
ANT 355 Law, Human Rights and Justice, ANT 340 Medical Anthropology, ANT 408 South Asian Society and Culture, fieldwork experience, a placement.
Teaching and the civil service
Schools and colleges; administrative and other cadres through public examinations; university teaching after a master's.
Depth in the core, EMB 101 and the Bangladesh courses (ECO 324; ANT 408), broad preparation alongside the degree.
Consulting, business and entrepreneurship
Business analysis, pricing, strategy, your own venture.
ECO 493 Industrial Organization, ECO 491 Introduction to Game Theory, ECO 331; for Anthropology ANT 210 and ANT 321 Economy and Society; an internship.
career_notes: Minor in Economics: 27 credits (24 core, 3 elective) on the department page - the course list is not published on the pages read. Minor in Anthropology: 27 credits - ANT 101, ANT 301, ANT 302 and ANT 375 (12 credits) plus five electives (15). Minor in Sociology: 24 credits - SOC 101, SOC 201 / ANT 202 and SOC 301 / ANT 203 (9 credits) plus five electives: three at the 300 level, one at the 400 level and one of your choice if it is a cross-listed ANT / SOC course. For Anthropology students the seven Courses Outside of Department 'can be a minor'; the Economics page prints no rule on open electives - ask your advisor before counting a minor course among the eleven.
Research routes, as each programme prints them

Economics has no internship course: research lives in ECO 499 Undergraduate Thesis ('a two semester long supervised thesis for the advanced undergraduate students', prerequisite 'Permission of Supervisor'), ECO 498 Independent Study (ECO 208, ECO 209) and the seminar papers of ECO 401 - all electives. Anthropology ends in a 4-credit choice, ANT 401 (b) Senior Thesis or ANT 402 (b) Senior Internship, after ANT 375 and ANT 376, finished inside one semester under the department's three-month timetable; students who enrolled before Spring 2026 take ANT 401 or ANT 402 at 3 credits.

programs.version_note: This is the curriculum printed on the programme page: 40 courses / 120 credit hours, split as General Education 13 courses / 39 credits, Core 16 / 48 and Electives 11 / 33. The page prints no curriculum version, intake year or duration in years; its RECOMMENDED COURSES list runs ten semesters (the 3rd marked "(RS)"), which is the n_semesters used here. The page prints no credit figure per course: the 3 on every ECO row is the category total divided by its course count (48/16 and 33/11), not a printed number, and ECO 499 Undergraduate Thesis ("two semester long") may carry a different value - confirm it. General Education rows and the stream rules come from the university's Streams and Courses page ("39 credits (13 courses)") that the programme page links to; that page prints no per-course credits either (the Anthropology programme page prints 3 for the same courses). Prerequisites are the ones printed under each course in Course Details. The page does not say how many of the eleven "Program/ Open Elective" slots may be open (non-Economics) courses and prints no list of open electives - copy those from your advising sheet.
facts: 120 credits = General Education 39 (13 courses) + Core 48 (16 courses) + Electives 33 (11 courses), printed as a table under "The areas, number of courses and credit hours required for graduation are given below:".

Core: 16 ECO courses from ECO 101 to ECO 432; ECO 101 needs MAT 101 and ECO 202 needs STA 101, so both Stream 2 GenEd courses come in the 1st semester of the recommended list; ECO 201 Mathematics for Business and Economics needs "MAT 101/ MAT 105/ MAT 110, ECO 101".

Electives: "the students also need to take Economics elective courses in various other fields", which the page groups into Microeconomics, Macroeconomics, Quantitative Methods, International Economics, Monetary and Financial Economics, Public Economics, Agriculture, Resource and Environmental Economics, Development Economics and Economic Growth and other special topics; 22 Program Elective Courses are listed and the recommended list has eleven "Program/ Open Elective" slots in the 7th to 10th semesters.

Most electives need ECO 208 and ECO 209 "(or permission of instructor)"; ECO 301 needs ECO 208, ECO 302 needs ECO 209 and ECO 201, ECO 307 needs ECO 201, ECO 401 needs ECO 303, ECO 430 needs ECO 202 and ECO 303, ECO 492 needs ECO 307.

ECO 499 Undergraduate Thesis is an elective, "a two semester long supervised thesis for the advanced undergraduate students", prerequisite "Permission of Supervisor"; ECO 498 Independent Study (prerequisite ECO 208, ECO 209) is the other research elective; no internship course is printed.

ECO 401 Research Methods in Economics and Social Sciences "will also be offered as SOC 401: Issues and Methods of Research" with modules for Sociology Minor students; ECO 303 Introduction to Econometrics requires "a small empirical research project using econometric software packages".

General Education (Streams and Courses page, "39 credits (13 courses)"): Stream 1 Writing Comprehension - any two of ENG 101, ENG 102, ENG 103; Stream 2 Math and Natural Sciences - minimum two; Stream 3 Arts and Humanities - BNG 103 and HUM 103 compulsory plus at least one more; Stream 4 Social Sciences - EMB 101 compulsory plus at least one more; Stream 5 Communities, Seeking Transformation - minimum one; plus three GenEd electives from Streams 2-5 or from outside the student's department.

The recommended list prints "ENG 101 / ENG 102" in the 1st semester and "ENG 102 / ENG 103" in the 3rd, each with an asterisk the page does not explain; the Freshman Enrollment page says the admission test prescribes ENG 101 English Fundamentals and/or ENG 102 English Composition (3 credits each) and the non-credit ENG 091, MAT 091 and MAT 092, up to four courses in the first semester.

"A student may also be required to take non-credit, remedial courses in English and Mathematics" (programme page); the Policies and Procedures page: "Courses numbered 001-099 are remedial or non-credit courses", with one retake allowed for 091/092 courses in the first or second semester.

The "3rd Semester (RS)" is the Residential Semester: the Residential Semester page describes it as the 3rd semester of undergraduate study at the Savar campus where students complete General Education courses (this plan puts HUM 103, EMB 101, ENG 102/ENG 103 and BNG 103 there); the Policies page says "Attending Residential semester is compulsory for all BRAC University students"; the Tuition and Fees page prints a residential semester fee of Tk. 90,000.

Admission (ESS Eligibility and Undergraduate Admission pages): "Minimum GPA of 3.50 in SSC/equivalent and HSC/equivalent separately (including additional subject)", or O-Levels GPA 2.5 in five subjects and A-Levels 2.5 in two ("Subjects with E Grade will not be considered"), or IB "Minimum DP Score of 24"; the admission test for BSS in Economics is "English (Composition and MCQ) and Mathematics MCQ", each sub-section passed separately, followed by an interview.

University rules (Policies and Procedures page): graduation needs "A minimum of 120 credits for a bachelor's degree out of which at least 70 must be earned at BRAC University", a CGPA of 2.00 and clearance from Accounts, Library and Registrar; a CGPA below 2.0 puts the student on probation with up to three consecutive semesters to recover; "The maximum period to complete the undergraduate program is eight years from the date of first admission" (minimum three years); after an F a course may be retaken twice with the best grade counting, and a passed course repeated once within two semesters with the latest grade counting.
Minor in Economics (department page): 27 credits, 24 core and 3 elective - the course list is not published on the pages read.

Fees (Tuition and Fees page, "Non-refundable fees for new students enrolled from Spring 2027", "All other Program" column - Economics is not named): tuition Tk. 8,250 per credit, semester fee Tk. 10,520, admission fee Tk. 33,900 (one time, includes one course), library membership fee Tk. 2,500 (one time), additional first-semester courses Tk. 24,750 each, first-semester total Tk. 71,670.
Three semesters a year - Spring, Summer and Fall (Academic Dates page: Spring 2026 classes from 31 Jan, Summer 2026 from 9 Jun, Fall 2026 from 3 Oct).

book.title: The ESS Degree Planner
book.subtitle: Department of Economics and Social Sciences, BRAC University
lines: Two degrees, one department: the 120-credit BSS in Economics and the 130-credit BSS in Anthropology, each on its own map with every printed prerequisite, the thesis route as each programme prints it, and a tracker that does the CGPA math on BRACU's own scale.
small: Programme structures, rules, fees and dates checked against BRAC University's official web pages (bracu.ac.bd) in October 2026.
Independent, unofficial study product. Not produced by, affiliated with or endorsed by BRAC University. Always confirm with the Office of the Registrar, your advisor and your department.

book.text: Read this first

This planner puts your whole ESS degree in one place: every published course, the rules that move your CGPA, the dates that cost money, and a working page for every week of the semester - on your phone, offline, with the arithmetic done for you.
What you are holding

items: **Degree** - the Bachelor of Social Science in Economics and Bachelor of Social Sciences in Anthropology as BRACU prints it: every course, its credits and its prerequisite. Pick a semester and a grade per course and the CGPA, the credit map, the Ready / Locked checks and your semester-by-semester plan follow.
**CGPA** - the grading scale, a quick semester GPA, what it takes to reach a target, a retake what-if on BRACU's own rule, and the CGPA lines that decide waivers and standing.
**Money** - this semester's bill at the published rates, the whole degree roughly, and the dates that cost money with a countdown you can send to your calendar.
**Semester** - deadlines and tasks, your routine with a clash check, and the working pages of a semester (set-up, course pages, check-ins, finals plan), one set per semester.
**Toolkit** - the tools this department's work actually needs, with logs and calculators that count and flag as you type.
**Rules** - BRACU's own grading, retake, probation, load, scholarship and fee rules, with the source named under each.
**More** - clubs and careers, the printable pages, an assignment cover page, the Excel version of the tracker, and your backup.

book.text: What it is not

items: It is **not an official BRACU document**. Nobody at the university wrote, checked or approved it.
It does **not replace your advisor**, your advising sheet or the student portal. Those decide what counts toward your degree.

It is **a snapshot**. Course lists, fees, CGPA lines and dates were read from BRACU's own web pages on 20 October 2026. Universities change these. When a notice and this planner disagree - cross the old line out here, and the notice wins.

book.text: Start in 15 minutes

items: On **Home**, type your name, the semester you were admitted in and the semester you are in now.
On **Degree**, pick the semester and the grade of every course you have passed. Your CGPA appears at once, and every course shows Ready, Locked or Open.
On **Money**, type this semester's fee and drop dates from the Registrar's calendar; they count down on Home.
On **Semester**, put your sections into the routine and your deadlines into the task list.
Open the **Toolkit** when the work starts: labs, projects, cases, the final-year runway.

book.text: Your data

Everything you type stays in this browser on this device - nothing is sent anywhere, there is no account and no internet is needed. That also means a cleared browser or a new phone starts empty. So, now and then, open **More** and tap **Save this planner with my data inside**: you get this same file back with everything you have typed written into it. Keep that copy - open it on a laptop, send it to a new phone, or hand it to next semester's you.

If a browser refuses to keep your data between visits (some phones open files in a way that forgets), Home tells you so and offers the same button. Your planner is then simply the latest copy you saved.

Most students learn these rules by breaking one. Read them once now. Everything here is taken from BRAC University's published pages as they stood in October 2026; the source is named under each section.
The grading scale
BRAC University's undergraduate scale, in force since Fall 2020. Both A+ and A carry the full 4.0.
A+ to D- are passing grades. F is failing: it earns no credit and counts as zero in your GPA.
How your GPA and CGPA are worked out

Every course gives you **quality points = credits x grade point**. Add the quality points for a semester and divide by the credits you attempted for a letter grade: that is your semester GPA. Do the same across all semesters and you have your CGPA. The policy page prints the same formula: the sum of (grade points x credits) over the credits attempted.
Three things students get wrong

items: **An F stays in the sum until it is retaken.** It adds credits to the bottom of the fraction and nothing to the top.
**A D- passes, but it costs you.** A 3-credit D- is 2.1 quality points against 12.0 for an A - and a grade of B- or below is what the repeat rule exists for.
**W, I, P and AU never enter the GPA.** A W costs you the fee and the semester's work, not grade points.
